extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity officers, science policymakers, and bibliometricians
extracted.subtask_description: Comprehensive bibliometric and qualitative analysis of retracted biomedical and life-science research articles, including classification of causes, temporal/geographic patterns, and recommendations for policy and practice to reduce misconduct and improve retraction transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Retraction (classification categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracted articles are classified according to whether the cause of retraction was documented fraud (data falsification or fabrication), suspected fraud, plagiarism, duplicate publication, error, unknown, or other reasons (e.g., journal error, authorship dispute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these discrete categories when coding retractions; some articles may fall into more than one category. The paper reports prevalence (e.g., fraud/suspected fraud 43.4%, error 21.3%, duplicate publication 14.2%, plagiarism 9.8%) and emphasizes that classification affects interpretation of trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secondary sources to ascertain cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices alone are often insufficient; additional sources (Office of Research Integrity reports, Retraction Watch, news media, public records, contacting authors) should be consulted to determine the true cause of retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors reclassified 158 articles after consulting secondary sources and note that relying solely on retraction notices can systematically underestimate fraud. Cross-checking decisions should be documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent review and consensus for classification decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each classification decision should be independently reviewed by multiple investigators and discrepancies resolved by consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reports that all classification decisions were independently reviewed by all authors and any discrepancies were resolved—this is a recommended quality-assurance step for retraction coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative retraction notices (transparency requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction announcements should be specific and detailed about the reason for retraction; many are currently incomplete, opaque, or author-written in ways that obscure misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents 119 instances with no information provided and argues for uniform standards requiring explicit, informative retraction notices so the literature and readers can correctly interpret the reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform standards/guidelines for retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should adopt consistent, uniform guidelines for content and format of retraction notices to improve transparency and comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because policies vary widely (some journals decline to provide explanations), establishing uniform guidelines is recommended to reduce systematic underestimation of misconduct and improve the value of retractions as a corrective mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized database of scientific misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Create and maintain a centralized repository/database documenting instances of scientific misconduct and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A centralized database is proposed to support consistent tracking, reduce opacity, and aid researchers, editors, and policymakers in identifying patterns and serial offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued access to retracted articles conditional on clear reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracted articles should generally remain accessible provided that they are accompanied by detailed descriptions regarding the reasons for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue continued access can be useful (e.g., for material of limited continuing value) but must be paired with detailed retraction explanations to prevent misuse or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of checklists by authors and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased use of checklists for authors and reviewers to reduce errors and improve reporting quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklists are proposed as one practical intervention to reduce retractions attributable to error or oversight; implementation details are not specified but are recommended as part of a package of reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved training in logic, probability, and statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhanced methodological training for scientists in logic, probability, and statistics to reduce errors and flawed inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper recommends stronger quantitative and critical-reasoning training as a preventive measure against retractions due to methodological error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced focus on ethics education
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger and more systematic ethics training for scientists to prevent misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethics education is listed as a necessary component but is unlikely alone to eliminate misconduct; it should be combined with structural reforms and oversight mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and national oversight for investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedicated national agencies (e.g., US Office for Research Integrity) and institutional processes are important for overseeing investigations of alleged misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors highlight the role of such agencies in supporting investigations and recommend their continued/strengthened use to identify and document misconduct; investigations can be lengthy (average ~20.5 months in ORI reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of journal-impact factor relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal-impact factor correlates with retractions for fraud and error but not (or only weakly) with plagiarism and duplicate publication; retractions for fraud/error are more common in higher-impact journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact factor can be used as an analytic variable to explore patterns but should not be overinterpreted; correlations may reflect scrutiny, incentives, or both. The paper provides statistical correlations (e.g., R^2 values) and recommends nuanced interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-to-retraction as an evaluative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the interval between publication and retraction (time-to-retraction); this varies by cause (fraud has substantially longer mean time-to-retraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time-to-retraction trends may reflect the length of investigations, discovery processes, and editorial behavior. The authors report mean months-to-retract by category (e.g., fraud mean ~46.8 months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor citation behavior of retracted articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Track citations to retracted articles to assess the effectiveness of retraction as a corrective action; some retracted articles continue to be cited as if valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation trajectories vary: some retracted articles show rapid citation decline, others continue to be cited. Monitoring citations can inform policy on marking retracted items and on continued access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and monitor serial offenders / author-level patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify authors or research groups responsible for multiple retractions, since a small number of groups can account for a large fraction of fraud retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents that 38 groups with ≥5 retractions accounted for ~43.9% of fraud retractions; recognizing cascades of retractions from single investigations is important for understanding overall trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret retraction counts as underestimates of true misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the number of retracted articles is a lower-bound estimate of fraudulent publications because many suspected fraudulent works remain unretracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are provided where evidence of fraud exists but few or no retractions were issued; analysts should account for underascertainment when drawing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address incentives and systemic reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms to the incentive structures of science (reduce winner-takes-all rewards; develop novel reward systems and more consistent funding) are needed to reduce incentives for misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that perverse incentives (disproportionate rewards for high-profile publications) contribute to misconduct and propose structural reforms alongside training and oversight measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological choices for bibliometric analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit methodological rules: search PubMed for retracted publications in a defined time/date; use Journal Citation Reports impact factors (5-y when available); assign small surrogate values for journals without IF; and supplement with web searches for ambiguous cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents concrete choices (e.g., using 2011 JCR IFs, assigning 0.1 to journals without IF) and the use of Google, Retraction Watch, ORI reports to augment PubMed-derived data; such transparency in methods is recommended for reproducibility.
